Principles, and Suggestions

Abstract
In recent times, the term AI ethics caught the attention among the
academics, legislators, developers, and among AI users to promote
ethical AI development. While countries in the North have led the
way in discussions about the direction of ethical and responsible
artificial intelligence development and deployment, perspectives
from developing countries like Bangladesh are underrepresented.
Based on 32 qualitative interviews with different stakeholders,
including machine learning practitioners, academic researchers,
and policymakers in the emerging AI ecosystem in Bangladesh,
this work closely examines the ongoing challenges and opportunities to ensure AI ethics in Bangladesh with emerging AI usage. In
Bangladesh, the government has not yet fully implemented measures to empower citizens with AI-related skills, policies, resources,
and data ethics, and a significant portion of the population lacks
knowledge in AI. In this paper, we are presenting the findings of
AI4Bangladesh project that intend to create the roadmap for ethical
AI in Bangladesh. We outline the core challenges, present situation,
and risks of AI for Bangladesh; propose seven AI ethics principles,
and offer suggestions to ensure a transparent, accountable, and fair
AI ecosystem for Bangladesh.

1 Introduction
Bangladesh is a densely populated country of about 170+ million
citizens located in South Asia. The country is primarily focused on
agriculture, but advancements in technology are starting to impact
many aspects of everyday life and provide fresh inspiration.The
country’s substantial population, coupled with its rapid technological advancement, positions it uniquely to leverage the potential
benefits of AI. However, such benefits can only be realized if appropriate regulatory measures are implemented to ensure safe and
responsible use. As an increasing number of individuals engage
with AI technologies, the establishment of robust ethical guidelines
is imperative to safeguard against potential misuse or unintended
consequences arising from the deployment of these advanced systems. Although artificial intelligence (AI) has existed for several
decades, its impact is only now becoming evident within the context
of our nation. AI technologies are increasingly integrated into various aspects of daily life, enhancing convenience and accessibility.
Prominent applications include ride-sharing platforms such as Uber
and Pathao, food delivery services like Foodpanda, and chatbots utilizing natural language processing (NLP) for the Bengali language.
Out of the population, 66.94 million (38.9 percent) people are active
internet users along with 44.70 million (26.0 percent) active social
media users [ 67]. Bangladesh government aims to achieve a lot
more than a cashless society and a futuristic Bangladesh with 5G
internet, smartphones, and high-speed internet adoption of 100%
by 2041 [13, 57]. According to Government AI Readiness Index 2023
which ranks governments on many indicators including strategic
vision for AI, innovation capacity, data and infrastructure maturity,
Bangladesh ranks 82 out of 193 countries [59].
Given AI’s potent revolutionary potential and significant influence across a wide range of societal spheres, there has been
much discussion regarding the underlying principles that ought
to guide its creation and application [ 29, 51, 54, 68, 77, 108]. The
subject of ethical AI has been covered in several studies [27, 42, 43],
particularly in systematic risks [ 19, 48, 73], and unexpected bad
outcomes like data bias or algorithmic bias [ 16, 69, 80, 100]. Numerous research studies have been conducted considering different
aspects of AI ethics. These include fairness [14, 38, 65, 74, 89], responsibility [37, 39, 50, 63, 75, 99], transparency and accountability
[24, 34, 85, 88, 95, 98].
The ethics framework from different countries was designed
to identify the ethical concerns raised by AI technologies that are
new or likely to arise shortly and describe the steps that can be
taken to mitigate them [30, 44, 45, 55, 72, 96, 97]. There is still more
disagreement about whether AI should be held to human standards
of accountability or if humans are supposed to have final authority
over technical creations [ 35]. India released its very first report

ICTD 2024, December 09–11, 2024, Nairobi, Kenya Mayeesha et al.
mentioning the challenges and recommendations in AI ethics in
2023 [9]. While the existing exploration of AI-related policies and
ethical frameworks are there to mitigate the risks caused by AI
systems and many countries maintain strong data protection laws
and dedicated government facilities, similar organizations have
not been created in countries like Bangladesh. For example, Office
of the Privacy Commissioner in Canada [ 78], National Artificial
Intelligence Initiative (NAII) and the AI Bill of Rights [6] in USA,
European Union (EU) AI act [8] in EU, AI Principles introduced in
China [20], AI guidelines of UK Government [36], Brazil’s AI regulations [53] facilitate and enact policies relating to AI in the respective
countries. However, South Asian nations, such as Bangladesh, are in
the preliminary stages of deliberating the necessity for AI-specific
regulations, with notable gaps in governance particularly evident
in regions where AI infrastructure remains underdeveloped despite
the rapid emergence of AI-driven applications.
The necessity for artificial intelligence (AI) ethics is growing as
we integrate AI systems more and more [11]. AI ethics are the moral
precepts that organizations apply to direct the ethical and responsible creation and deployment of AI. There is no field left where AI
is not leaving its footprints, from space exploration to autonomous
cars [70, 107]. Given AI’s potent revolutionary potential and significant influence across a wide range of societal spheres, there has been
much discussion regarding the underlying principles that ought
to guide its creation and application [ 29, 51, 54, 68, 77, 108]. The
subject of ethical AI has been covered in several studies [27, 42, 43],
particularly in systematic risks [ 19, 48, 73], and unexpected bad
outcomes like data bias or algorithmic bias [16, 69, 80, 100].
South and Central Asia ranks second lowest among regions when
it comes to AI readiness [ 59]. However, many countries in Asia
including Bangladesh, India, China, Vietnam, Indonesia, and more
have published their AI-related strategy and initiatives to maximize
the benefits of AI to society along with growing the AI ecosystem
[60]. Prior work has focused on perspectives such as power asymmetries and inequalities, western regulatory monopolies, commercial
exploitation of foreign companies, concerns related to human rights
and harms associated with the labor and material supply chains of
AI infrastructure [21, 76, 82], AI-related policy analysis of South
Asia, particularly Bangladesh has not been addressed before. Previous research has also shown that user attitudes and concerns
regarding ethics vary greatly in the South based on factors such
as culture, religion, geography, and infrastructure-related issues
[66, 102]. As a result, it is important to contextualize AI ethics research in the local context and take into account differing values to
close the technological gaps in capability and resources [25, 26].
Following the implementation of AI strategies [17] of Bangladesh
for three years from 2019, several issues still exist (1) infrastructural
gaps; (2) Scarcity of accessible and high-quality data; (3) A proficient labor force in AI skills; (4) Ethical and legal structures; and (5)
Development and research [32, 52]. Bangladesh recently drafted a
"National Artificial Intelligence Policy" [12] in 2024 where significant potential for AI adaptation in different sectors including public
services in Bangladesh was identified. Multiple priority sectors such
as smart public services, telecommunication, data governance and
surveillance, agriculture, environment, energy and climate change,
smart city, education, healthcare have been considered in the national policy, however no regulatory or ethics framework currently
has been formed. Before such ethical or regulatory frameworks are
created, it is important to find the current state of the AI ecosystem
and the priorities various stakeholders find as crucial. To address
such concerns, we initiated our study with the following questions.
• RQ1 What is the current State of AI-related policies in
Bangladesh?
– RQ1.1 What are the major potential risk areas associated
with the development or application of AI products in
Bangladesh?
– RQ1.2 What measures are necessary to foster the growth
of the AI ecosystem in Bangladesh?
• RQ2 What are the concerns surrounding the introduction
of regulatory and ethical principles in Bangladesh, and what
is the potential for adapting and creating such principles in
the local context?
The full procedure of developing the AI4Bangldesh project consists of 3 cycles. In cycle 1 we studied AI ethics framework, principles, and related works from different regions, AI ethics guidelines
and concerns, current AI regulatory systems, national AI strategy, and the digital security act of Bangladesh. We have done the
qualitative study with 32 interviews including - policymakers, stakeholders, academicians, and developers in the phase of cycle 2 to
understand and to know more about the current situation of AI
and user experiences to develop our AI4Bangladesh project. In
cycle 3 we contextualized our findings from the interviews and
proposed seven principles in this paper to serve as an ethical guideline to direct organizations while using or developing AI systems
in Bangladesh. We present our findings initially highlighting key
issues such as AI risks in local context, data ethics and protection, concerns related to AI regulation and perception of AI ethics
principles from our stakeholders viewpoint.
The contribution of this paper lies in exploring the current state
of AI and possibilities for developing an adequate ethical framework
considering the existing concerns. This work can be of interest of
regions that are developing AI ethical frameworks within limited
resources. In our work we highlight following contributions :
• Identification of Critical Knowledge Gaps and Challenges : Through in-depth interviews with 32 stakeholders,
our research highlights significant knowledge gaps and challenges in AI ethics research in Bangladesh, include concerns
on data protection, humanitarian issues such was wage disparities of annotators and lack of awareness of general population. These findings highlight the urgent need for targeted
interventions and policy initiatives to promote responsible
and equitable AI development.
• Acknowledgement and perspectives around AI Ethics
Principles from Stakeholders : This paper presents the
stakeholder perceptions of seven AI ethics principles and
the emphasis on key concerns such as fairness, explainability, accountability as well as highlighting region specific
needs such as demand for independent oversight due to concerns around government surveillance. This will provide a
valuable guide for policymakers, researchers and industry
practitioners.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section
2 presents the background of our work, Section 3 represents the

methodology, Section 4 details the findings derived from the interviews. Finally, Section 5 offers the suggested principles and compares them with prior work.
2 Background
Around the world, countries are actively formulating AI-related
policies and ethical frameworks to address the potential risks associated with artificial intelligence systems. In many cases, nations
in the Global North have established robust data protection laws
and dedicated governmental bodies to oversee AI governance.
In contrast, countries in South Asia, such as Bangladesh, are at an
early stage in recognizing the necessity of laws specifically tailored
to AI governance. When designed in the North, AI and data-driven
systems are often presumed to be value-neutral; however, these
systems inherently reflect the values and biases of their creators. In
prior work the impact of colonialism in AI ethics research has been
discussed, which manifests through the imposition of values and
frameworks developed in the Global North onto the Global South,
disregarding local contexts and perpetuating power imbalances.
This results in technologies that prioritize profit over addressing
region-specific needs, often reinforcing historical patterns of exploitation and control. [ 31, 33, 83]. A pertinent example is Facebook’s content moderation system [90], where algorithms designed
for Western contexts are applied universally, often disregarding
local nuances. To ensure responsible and equitable AI deployment,
these technologies must be adapted to reflect the unique needs and
cultural contexts of the Global South.
In the realm of AI governance, South Asian countries are at an
early stage of recognizing the need for specialized AI policies, while
many Western nations are already in the process of implementing comprehensive frameworks. In Bangladesh, there are ongoing
efforts to draft AI policies and a data protection act aimed at safeguarding consumer data [5]. However, these proposed regulations
are still in their preliminary stages, and the lack of robust data
protection laws has led to significant public concerns over business
practices and potential violations of human rights. Furthermore,
the existing Digital Security Act of 2018 has been widely criticized
for its controversial implications regarding freedom of expression
and misuse [ 4, 71]. The current AI ecosystem in Bangladesh is
comprised of various stakeholders, including government agencies,
private sector companies, and academic researchers. Despite this
growing landscape, there has been no dedicated research on AI
ethics, nor have there been any government-led initiatives to establish ethical AI guidelines. This highlights the urgent need for
a comprehensive AI governance framework to manage the risks
associated with AI deployment in the country [15, 104].
The current state of AI ethics research in Bangladesh is still in
its nascent stage, with limited but growing academic and policyfocused activities. Key themes include algorithmic fairness, inclusivity, bias mitigation, and responsible AI for the Global South. The
current state of AI ethics and policy research in Bangladesh is evolving, particularly with the introduction of the National Artificial
Intelligence Policy 2024 [12]. This policy aims to address various
social, legal, and ethical issues related to AI implementation across
sectors such as education, healthcare, and agriculture. However, it
lacks comprehensive guidelines for critical areas like national security and organized cyber crime using generative AI technologies,
which raises concerns about its effectiveness in mitigating risks
associated with AI technologies.
The prior research focus has been on understanding AI’s social
and cultural impacts, such as how language models may handle
local societal norms, as well as addressing challenges like misinformation, content moderation and authorship of AI research [102].
The government and academic communities are increasingly aware
of the need for AI ethics frameworks. Some efforts, like policy drafts
and workshops, aim to establish guidelines for the ethical use of AI
in public and private sectors. However, concrete regulatory measures and comprehensive datasets to support these initiatives are
still lacking. Bangladesh is also witnessing a gradual expansion
of interdisciplinary research, combining insights from computer
science, social sciences, and policy-making. However, the research
landscape remains under-resourced, and ethical AI initiatives are
still fragmented, with most developments focusing on policy recommendations rather than practical implementations or technical
solutions. Overall, the field is evolving but requires more support
for broader adoption and deeper, context-specific research.
The present study aims to initiate foundational research on AI
ethics within the Bangladeshi context to investigate public perceptions regarding AI policies, including their level of awareness,
knowledge gaps, and preferences for policy frameworks. By adopting an academic lens, this research seeks to identify the specific
regulatory needs and expectations of local stakeholders, ultimately
contributing to the formulation of future AI policies for Bangladesh
and other countries at a similar stage of responsible AI development.
3 Methodology
We conducted semi-structured, in-depth, open ended interviews
with prominent domain experts spanning multiple domains to obtain their perspective on the current state and future of AI ethics
in Bangladesh. Our methodology is described below in following
sections - consideration of expert interviews as our method, creation of our interview topic guide and questionnaire, recruitment
of participants, conducting interviews and analysis of our findings.
Expert Interviews: Talking to experts in the exploratory phases
helps to collect concentrated data efficiently compared to other
methods such as quantitative surveys or participatory observations.
Expert interviews can serve as a surrogate for broader community and offer useful insider knowledge [ 28]. In the context of
Bangladesh the context of AI ethics is unfamiliar to broader population, thus the choice of expert interviews was driven by the need
to capture in-depth, nuanced understandings of AI ethics within
our specific sociopolitical and technological context. Expert interviews have some limitations such as the fact expert perspectives
may be biased by their own experiences or may not fully capture
the diversity of perspectives [ 40], To combat this issue initially
we identified various stakeholders, including government officials
who have experience in research and deployment in AI based applications, machine learning engineers and founders of ML-focused
companies in Bangladesh and academic researchers working in
various domains including computer vision, natural language processing, machine learning theory and human computer interaction.

We also aimed to identify and interview experts who have worked
with marginalized groups, for example, one of our participants was
an accessibility researcher focused on disabled community working with government and another worked in deploying Bengali
natural language processing tools to Bangladeshi population. Many
of our participants directly worked with marginalized population
for data collection or development of AI based products for them.
Thus we believe our expert voices speak for the broader population
in Bangladesh. While the format of the expert interviews were
semi-structured, interviewers asked relevant follow-up questions
to explore the topics respondents wanted to expand upon in depth.
Interview Guide Creation : A semi-structured interview guide
was developed to ensure consistency across interviews while allowing flexibility for participants to elaborate on topics of particular
importance or relevance to their experience, where participants
were able to adhere to open-ended questions according to their
expertise. The topics considered are following -
• Perception of participants on the current AI ecosystem in
Bangladesh,
• Participant perspective of state of AI ethics in Bangladesh,
• Their opinions on whether AI should be regulated and what
sort of regulations should be introduced,
• Opinion on data protection and privacy related concerns in
Bangladesh,
• Participant considerations of AI ethics related concepts such
as FATE(Fairness, accountability,Transparency and Explainability) and how they wish for them to be introduced in our
local context,
• Risks and harms which might be created by AI systems in
this context,
• Necessary measurements to grow the AI ecosystem in Bangladesh,
• Creation and adaptation of context specific AI ethics framework in Bangladesh.
Participant Recruitment: We interviewed 32 participants and
our respondents were selected from a broad variety of fields. The
respondents were from the field of computer science (6), Law and
Policy (7), Ethics Researcher (2), Machine Learning Engineer (4),
Telecom Industry (6), XAI researcher (1), HCI Researcher (1), Machine Learning Consultant (2), Accessibility Researcher (1), Academic and Administrator of Government of Bangladesh (1). All
respondents had a minimum of 2 to a maximum of 15 years of
experience in working with AI. Among 32 respondents 23 were
male and 9 were female based in Europe (1), Canada (1), the UK (1),
India (1), and the rest of the 28 were from Bangladesh. Combining
open-ended interviews with a reading of the literature assists in
assembling a more thorough image of Bangladesh’s AI ecosystem.
Selection Process: Purposive sampling was used to identify and
select domain experts in AI in Bangladesh [91]. Participants were
chosen based on multiple criterias such as significant academic or
professional achievement in domains related to AI, deep understanding of the challenges of creating, deploying and regulating
AI and technology focused applications and track record demonstrated through publications, public speaking, or leadership roles
in relevant organizations. We aimed to interview broadly, such
as reaching out to regulation related executives of large telecom
companies or prominent ICT lawyers with expertise to ensure perspectives of stakeholders have a wide range. Finding and choosing
specialists with the necessary experience was an iterative process
till completion. We contacted the participants via email and their
social media platforms. In total over fifty people were contacted,
out of which we received responses from 32.
Interview Procedure: Involvement in the study was entirely
voluntary. The goal of the interview was explained to the respondents, who were also given some background information and
examples emphasizing the importance of accountability and ethics
in AI systems. We hold the meetings in both in-person and online
mode as per the participant’s preference. Due to the semi-structured
nature of the interviews, the same general questions were asked
of each participant, however we asked follow up questions based
on the participant responses. The nature of the interviews was
individual and focus group by the participant’s preferences and
availability. The interviews were conducted mostly in Bengali (the
preferred language of the participants) apart from the ones who
were from outside of Bangladesh. For them, the interviews were in
English. Notes and recordings was taken during the interview in
front of the respondents with their consent. The interviews lasted
40-60 minutes each. 11 of the interviews were offline and the rest
were online.
Evaluation and Theme Generation: We used inductive approach [94] to analyzed the data. After carefully going over the
transcripts, we created categories, groups, and sub-groups of passages that best represented the main ideas in the data. Based on
the theme we have created our code book [86] with five main categories (AI risks, data ethics, AI regulation, FATE perspectives, and
solutions) and several sub-categories (likely- knowledge gap, data
misuse, unavailability of resources, diversity and so on). The interview taken in Bengali was also translated into English in this phase
to generate the themes.
Research Ethics: Strong research ethics have been maintained
throughout the study. Since our inquiry was delicate, we took considerable effort to ensure respondent confidentiality and anonymity.
Participants received details about the study’s objectives, types of
inquiries, and researcher affiliations during the invitation-only process. In order to preserve their privacy, we did not record any
information about their identity, and before each interview, verbal
consent was obtained. Participants were free to end the interview at
any time if they were uncomfortable for any reason. The participant
was free to decline to answer any question as well.
4 Findings from Interviews
4.1 AI Risks in Local Context
Participants in our interviews were more concerned with risks
that were contextualised locally. For example, they cared about
protecting users from harmful applications of AI that originated in
the north, ensuring fairness in protecting marginalised communities
from a variety of AI applications, and upholding the human rights
of labourers who worked with data, such as annotators, to ensure
inclusivity.
4.1.1 Knowledge Gap Among Diverse Stakeholders. : Many participants noted that among policymakers AI is still a "buzzword" and

even business owners and investors often think AI is a"magical tool
that can do anything" . However, same policymakers will eventually
produce regulations and policies regarding AI, so this knowledge
gap could potentially become a significant problem. Again, other
stakeholders brought up the issue of that sometimes we produce
machine learning applications without consulting appropriate domain expertise, such as one example where the participant noted
creating AI products relating to female reproductive health without
consulting medical doctors or gender researchers.
Our participants proposed a number of ideas to address the
problems caused by this knowledge gap, including identifying skill
and knowledge gaps, adding mandatory AI-related lessons to the
national education curriculum, providing policymakers with AI-
related training and awareness programs, enhancing the teaching
of math and computer science in our universities. Notably, there
was a concern to enhance AI literacy among legal professionals and
policymakers. Other stakeholders noted that working with ICT and
education ministries to facilitate training for current teachers and
policymakers is perhaps the quickest way to increase AI literacy
in Bangladesh. Creating user-friendly AI products to improve customer satisfaction and ensuring media participation in discussions
on AI-related products and policies was also suggested.
4.1.2 Lack of Infrastructure and Policy Relating to AI. : Although a
national AI strategy draft has been released, as discussed previously,
our participants urgently pointed out that it is extremely difficult
to legally protect ourselves against AI-specific risks and harms in
Bangladesh because there is currently no policy, regulation, or set
of standardised guidelines focused on AI. They also mentioned
the challenges of deploying AI based products without appropriate infrastructure in place. For example, a participant mentioned
"We can diagnose traffic violations by adding a computer vision system, we don’t have the overall infrastructure to manage it" citing
the existing issues such as poor maintenance of during previous
implementations of automated traffic systems. Participants from
Government projects for Natural language processing also mentioned challenges associated with deployment and accessibility as
machine learning applications are often computational resource
intensive in deployment. Mentioning a major book trade market
of Dhaka, a participant noted "Nilkhet shopkeepers, compositors in
Banglabazar do not have the access of high end devices. We need to
understand and negotiate with their requirements and configurations
for bangla.gov projects". Another participant noted the importance
of creating AI applications that enriches and preserves Bangladeshi
culture and heritage.
According to our participants, AI companies in Bangladesh mainly
earn by consulting and freelancing while very few having their
own products. Even if companies wanted to start AI businesses in
Bangladesh, there are still obstacles to overcome. For example, GPU
pricing are unstable in Bangladesh, there isn’t a server-grade, highquality vendor, and local students find it difficult to obtain credit
cards for research or GPU purchases due to insufficient funds and
bank regulations. The majority of students in Bangladesh utilise
the cracked versions of paid software, which is unethical but if
they are barred from using it, many of them might not be able to
complete the assignments. GPU insufficiency is a large barrier of
Bangladesh and developers find it hard to create and deploy ML
products. Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) dependent machine learning is expensive and subject
to multiple regulations from government, such as user data must
remain in Bangladesh for example [ 5]. Cash flow in Bangladesh
often comes for ML consulting companies by working with less
regulated countries like Myanmar according to our participants,
but the ethics surrounding it has not been addressed.
In order to guarantee that AI is created and applied responsibly,
collaboration among academics and the tech sector is becoming
more and more crucial and ought to be given priority. Governments should fund ethics and social understanding of technology
so that people get inspired to study more on this topic. Additional
funding from universities given to research projects carried out
in collaboration with industry and make long-term investments
in vital, cutting-edge research infrastructure to guarantee that our
academics have readily available the resources they require.
4.1.3 Major Risk Areas in Bangladesh Context. Upon being asked
about perspectives on highest risks AI applications in Bangladesh
context, stakeholders initially mentioned that "risk related standardizations" need to be discussed further to come to a better understanding. Considering the current unstable political situation
in Bangladesh, one participant highlighted the detrimental effects
of rumours and misinformation generated by chatgpt or similar
LLMs. Fake news or the dissemination of misinformation was thus
identified as a major area of danger from our participants. Prior
work also emphasized the importance of prioritizing research on
Bangla fake news [58, 61]. Generating images with Deepfake had
raised another major concern from participants as one noted"Deep-
Fake generated content should be regulated strictly. In our cultural
and religious context if someones image is used to make pornographic
content, their life will be living hell" . Another executive from our
participants noted
"In Bangladesh context, there was a case before where
a woman gave 7 crores taka to a dorbesh (fake saint).
We have ’Jiner badsha’((king of genies) in our culture.
Add deepfake to it and we will see losses in many levels.
Potential for the negative consequence is very high. "
Participants also voiced concerns about job loss as a result of
automation related to AI, in addition to generative AI. According
to one attendee, artificial intelligence is creating new employment
like "data annotator" even if robots replace some existing ones.
While some participants voiced concern that Bangladesh’s textile
industries will heavily exploit AI to replace labourers, the majority
were optimistic about the technology’s potential to empower more
people by providing more jobs. They asked to focus on short term
or immediate risks such as labor exploitation’s of data annotators
as expanded upon in the following section 3.2. how changes made
in AI products in north can immediately impact our citizens men.
4.2 Data Ethics
4.2.1 Protecting marginalized communities during data curation.
Data collection, curation and annotation is the fundamental part
of AI model creation process. Researchers and machine learning
industry practitioners both collect data for ML model training in
Bangladesh. Concerns about data curation also included privacy
and annotation-related issues. One participant put aptly, "We don’t

like to spend money to collect data. We like to crawl data or steal them. "
indicating the practice of misusing personal or public data, ignoring
copyright laws and not providing appropriate renumeration during
training data collection for both foreign and local companies. Citing
the recent collection of speech data for Bengali [ 18] one participant noted the need for a data protection law that ensures foreign
companies are appropriately held accountable for using local data
and ensure appropriate payment - "Think about speech, we are making CommonVoice dataset, they will take this dataset, make models,
and charge us dollars" , while another participant mentioned even
non-profit organizations often curate data but they do not properly
acknowledge or pay the data providers - "NGO’s often provide very
small payment for data like paying 5 taka or food to poor people...in
Chittagong hill tracts indigenous people and Uttarbanga people were
concerned on such eyewashing attempts by companies. "
However, many machine learning practitioners and researchers
from our participants also mentioned following good practices voluntarily. To create products for users with low/no tech literacy,
many companies in Bangladesh have focused on speech related
products and voice data curation. Attempts to balance male-female
gender, different dialects and ethnicity related voice ratio during
curation of speech dataset to maintain diversity, minimize bias and
ensure fairness was mentioned by our participants. Researchers
similarly noted taking appropriate consent, IRB approval, proper
data anonymization and removal upon request during collection
of human data for biomedical or similar machine learning projects.
It should be noted that these voluntary efforts were performed by
trained academic researchers and engineers and is not the widespread norm in the machine learning community in general.
Data annotation is a fundamental part of training data curation
for supervised machine learning projects. Several participants mentioned the risks associated with the rise of data annotation firms
in Bangladesh and the lack of any minimum wage related law for
data annotators. One participations mentioned that a regulatory
body that can ensure a minimum wage for the data annotators can
avoid a potential "race to the bottom" where annotators have to
compete with Indian or other countries in global south to provide
data annotation for minimal payment. One AI ethics researcher
participant argued that "In UK whose who do freelancing they are
from very privileged background, but in Bangladesh the people who
do freelancing come from very under-privileged background. Data
annotation is a very long and time intensive work which can impact their mental health. Even if the work is being done by Indian
or Bangladeshi workers, we can not claim that the annotation has
embedded these communities values in that dataset, because the annotation guidelines came from north. " Recent studies based in India
also highlights pressures and inherent challenges related to data
annotation work having low cost annotations at high quality along
with ensuring work satisfaction and upward mobility for the annotators. Since data annotation work in Bangladesh is at an inception
phase, authorities can be prepared to set the industry up for success
and escape avoidable risks.
4.2.2 Protecting Individual Rights through Data Protection Law. In
an effort to safeguard personal data and address privacy-related
issues, numerous nations throughout the world have passed their
own versions of data protection laws or acts, including GDPR from
EU [1], Canada [ 2], India [ 7], China [ 3], Nigeria [ 10] and many
more. Many of these are in development phase, some have already
passed legal jurisdictions and currently in effect. Bangladesh also
has a "Data Protection Bill" in draft from 2022 which has not yet
been enacted [5]. However, our participants considered the current
draft as "vague and lacking" and asked for a clear, comprehensive
and well-scoped law. While responses related to AI specific regulation were mixed, all participants voted unanonymously for having
stronger data protection related regulation in the country. One
participant advocated "We need a data protection law that restricts
foreign companies from using Bangladeshi data" in order to ensure
more compensation for training data curation from local people.
Executives from major telecommunication companies mentioned
in order to provide more machine learning specific features to accommodate consumer needs a clear data protection law will help.
The Data Protection Act, or DPA, is the first data privacy-related
law to be proposed in Bangladesh; however, because of its vague
definition of personal data, limitations on businesses’ ability to
transfer data across borders, and policies related to data localization specifically keeping sensitive data inside Bangladesh, it has
also drawn significant criticism and scrutiny from stakeholders.
Claims were made that that the localization of data as specified in
the draft law would seriously increase the risk of monitoring and
human rights abuses [22, 93, 101]. Our participants also mentioned
that requirements such as user data must be stored in servers in
Bangladesh restricts innovation since there is a lack of Amazon or
Google Cloud scale data center providers in Bangladesh currently.
Participants asked for laws that follow international standards and
synchronize with other countries in Asia specifically due to trade
related requirements. Many of our participants also mentioned
personally while they have given feedback, due to a lack of synchronization between different stakeholders while drafting the data

4.3 AI Regulation and Audit Concerns
Key artefacts for an ethical professional practise in machine learning are regulations, such as formal norms, rules, and laws, and they
frequently result from discussions and debates that take ethical considerations into account. However regulations frequently clash with
how they are actually implemented. Our data analysis reveals that
while there is a need for such standardisation for policy implementation for many stakeholders and AI professionals in Bangladesh
context, the lack of synchronization among politicians, businessmen, academic researchers, ordinary users, and policymakers make
it difficult to implement AI regulation in Bangladesh.
4.3.1 Call for Supportive Regulatory Policies. A number of participants expressed unhappiness with Bangladesh’s earlier national AI
plan draft, noting the need to build new policies through participatory design and gather input from stakeholders at all levels. One
participant strongly noted "There is already an AI strategy report
in Bangladesh which is made by a private company without taking
consultation from academic stakeholders...They also did not consider
general peoples values and principles into account". He recommended
to initiate a participatory design for policy making including academic researchers, industry practitioners and voices of the citizens.
Participants called for "standardization" of AI-related legislation out of concern that regulations related to AI might be easily
abused and harm Bangladesh’s emerging AI industry. One of our
participants, a machine learning researcher and consultant strongly
expressed “The greatest problem with any sort of regulation in our
country is that any regulation can be misused. As a practitioner I
would rather not be regulated at all than be harmed. ” Similar opinion was voiced by an ICT lawyer,“Regulation is okay, but too much
regulation is going to hurt company interests” . While participants addressed the concerns for protecting user interests, they also wanted
to support the small and emerging Bangladesh AI ecosystem and
expressed sentiments that complex regulations will hurt innovation.
However, there was an interest in regulating the products that are
coming from north.
“There should be two types of regulation - regulation of
the global north related products in global south and
how we can regulate south related players. But right
now we do not have any major player in our country for AI...Majority AI regulations if implemented in
Bangladesh will be financially prohibitive for Bangladeshi
companies ”
Participants emphasized that AI related regulation in Bangladesh
should be simple, considerate of our culture and with a focus to
foster the growing AI ecosystem.
4.3.2 Call for Independent Oversight and Auditing. Our participants
recommended to initiate a participatory policy design process including academic researchers, industry practitioners and of course,
general citizens. One participant reminded us about the need for
having participation from civil society and media while regulating
AI products. Furthermore, they asked that penalties related to violation of regulation should be decided by experts and ministry
and be designed to adapt over culture, time and necessity. As a
recurring topic among our participants was their concern of regulations being misused, they requested that academics, research
teams, or other similar auditing organisations collaborate to create
an auditing system tailored to the local cultural setting in order to
win over practitioners.
While some participants maintained self-audit reports and internal audit teams for their products to address concerns related
to data privacy or customer rights, and some even seek advice
from third-party audit companies from Europe, our participants
observed that these practices are not the norm in Bangladesh. They
expressed a desire to create a culture of accountability and auditing
in Bangladesh noting "We want to create a culture where I go to a
company and I can ask what are the experiments you have done, what
are the results and so on" . Some of the participants made it clear

4.4 Stakeholder Perspectives on FATE
The viewpoints of the stakeholders on the fundamental AI ethical
concepts of fairness, accountability, transparency and explainability
are highlighted in this section.
4.4.1 Fairness. Fairness was a point of consideration by some of
our participants as they have actively worked with machine learning projects as engineers or researchers, however, majority of them
possessed very little or no knowledge about this concept. As majority of the non-technical stakeholders did not have adequate
knowledge of fairness related issues even if a significant amount
of work has already been done in the global south and the north
[23, 47, 87, 106]. However, many of our participants mentioned ensuring diversity and attempts to protect marginalized users while
data collection for machine learning applications as seen in section
3.2.1.
4.4.2 Accountability. Participants mentioned since there is no current AI regulation policy in enforcement in Bangladesh, current
accountability in Bangladesh is user-centric. Companies can generally offer products and the liability is held by users. There is
no direct law related to AI specific harm, but legal systems can
use existing ICT-centric laws to possibly address issues such as
data leakage or privacy concerns. Some of the participants depmanded a seperate policy section in the constitution aside from
data protection act regarding AI risks. Another participant raised
his concern about using the same accountability structures in all
regions. Depending on geography or culture protected minorities
differ a lot. He believed that systems need to be evaluated in their
geographic, ethnic, and cultural context. Stakeholders are not very
knowledgeable about accountability and were not as inclined to
discuss it.
4.4.3 Transparency. One of our participants, a researcher actively
working in global South ethics emphasized on making public policy
design process more transparent with multiple stages of revision
and considered transparency of policy making as different from
transparency of AI related systems. For model-level transparency
there was an interest in looking at what initiatives have been taken
in west, India and other countries. Other participants noted that
concepts of privacy is dependent on culture, and thus transparency
related questions can vary in our local context if we investigate further. Currently in Bangladesh there is no practice of general ethical
considerations for basic software and hardware-related projects
while challenges of AI transparency are complex. There was no
discernible interest in transparency or discussion of this subject
among the remaining participants.
4.4.4 Explainability. One of our participants, who works as an XAI
researcher in the user-centric explainability, raised significant concern about Bangladesh’s AI explainability. He added that though
there is work on XAI mostly in India [41, 49, 79], no work has been
done so far in Bangladesh. He also added that not only end users but
even when it comes to AI researchers, are not aware of explainability at all, "End users do not understand the term explainability, so we
have to use some other word. Depending on the context, we often have
to explain the term explainability by relating to different examples or
ideas. We ask questions like if they understand the predictions of the
AI system". Explainability was described as the degree to which a
different participant understood the overall structure of the system
and the working of the AI models behind the applications. Different
users need different explainability methods, as stated in the previous work [62]. Participants from the government sector admitted
that there is no specific expectation around model explainability
in Bangladesh. The rest of the participants from the stakeholder
group were not familiar with explainability at all.
5 Suggested AI Ethics Principles
Utilizing AI is a great tool with a wide range of applications. As
businesses and government organizations rely more on AI systems and automated decision-making, moral dilemmas are already
emerging that need to be resolved. Responding thoughtfully and
promptly is necessary, as this has major implications for the economic well-being, fundamental rights, and everyday life of every
Bangladeshi. Based on the codebook (details in Section 2) and our
findings (details in Section 3), we are proposing AI4Bangladesh a
roadmap with principles to ensure the ethical use, deployment, and
development of AI in Bangladesh.
(1) Individual Rights. AI systems must follow the do no harm
policy and must be created with the intention of not hurting or misleading people, and it must be applied in a way
that minimises potential negative impacts in terms of data
misuse and data integrity. AI system should ensure that
consumers receive advantages that outweigh the expenses.
Furthermore, AI systems must intact privacy of people’s personal data. It also needs to prevent data breaches that could
affect someone’s reputation or cause them psychological,
financial, professional, or other kinds of harm.
(2) Lawfulness. AI systems must abide by all applicable laws,
rules, and obligations of Bangldesh local and International
governments guidelines. The use of AI should be legal and
regulated by formal announced rules.
(3) Fairness and inclusivity. The training data should be free
from biases and should include all voices including the minorities and the marginalized communities to adapt to context and cultures. Outliers should also be considered to prevent model’s unfair treatment against people, communities,
or groups e.g., religious minorities , social minorities, indigenous community, political minority, economic minority
people who are living the below the poverty line, also the
women and elderly people who are technologically behind.
(4) Transparency and Explainability. Anytime an algorithm
goes into effect that affects a person, that person has to
be informed. Users need to have a clear and meaningful
information about AI systems and its deployment. AI systems
should ensures all information in a meaningful way which
is accessible and understandable by its relevant audiences.

The principles, rationale behind such principles, and corresponding recommendations are presented in Table 1. The proposed principles expand on conventional AI ethics frameworks by emphasizing
the inclusion of literacy and awareness, as well as a stronger focus
on inclusivity to address unique regional challenges in Bangladesh.
While established principles such as individual rights, lawfulness,
fairness, transparency, and explainability remain central, the addition of literacy and awareness aims to equip citizens with the
knowledge required to engage meaningfully with AI systems. Furthermore, the emphasis on inclusivity ensures that AI policies are
reflective of diverse societal needs, thereby fostering a more equitable AI ecosystem in contexts with varying levels of technological
maturity. The recommendations provided often have deeper concerns or possible implications with respect to a developing country
like ours with a large population without adequate technology
exposure, as we share here through a few examples. Bangladesh
AI Strategy 2024 identifies following principles - fairness and social equity, transparency and accountability, safety, security and
robustness, partnership and collaboration and human centered AI
[12]. However our focus on inclusivity, context-sensitiveness and
adapting to local cultures have not been prioritized adequately.
Upon review of 84 AI ethics guidelines in 2019, Jobin [64] found
that five AI ethics principles were the most common - transparency,
justice and fairness, non-maleficence, responsibility, and privacy.
Justice and responsibility converge towards accountability from our

In a review of non-western AI ethics guidelines [56], the authors
argued that some global values are generally present in all AI ethics
guidelines over the world, such as accountability, fairness, or transparency, however, the non-western guidelines should not neglect
their own cultural roots. The research recommended to "a thorough
study of the cultural presuppositions of each culture" to ground and
adapt the AI ethics principles to their own context. We believe our
work in this aspect, where we interviewed multiple stakeholders is
a small step in this direction in terms of grounding the AI ethics of
Bangladesh.
Interestingly, current research on AI ethics principles in East
Asia [105], while being conducted completely independently from
ours, suggested principles that are very similar to what our stakeholders prescribed such as - cultural consideration and sensitivity,
inclusivity, Transparency and accountability etc. They added additional principles such as Silk Road AI Renaissance, but in our
case, such economic-related principles will have to be contextualized in our economy or political context. Another important aspect
of our participants was their consistent mention of independent
oversight along with government supervision. In the recent rise
of surveillance by authorities, personal information is hard to protect. The vulnerability increases in regions like Bangladesh, where
data protection laws are not in place. In the recent Quota protest
2024 in Bangladesh, authorities used surveillance tactics such as
internet shutdown, nationwide curfew and monitoring of internet
traffic to identify student protesters [ 81]. The participants have
lived through multiple political uprisings and believe the existence
of independent organizations for AI auditing should be considered
alongside authorized government supervision.
Regarding risk assessment, AI application-generated content,
such as deep fake, may cause a greater risk to marginal communities unaware of such possibilities. As we are far behind in having
adequate laws around AI and ethics, it is required to design one
that is consistent with existing legal framing and cultural context
to protect ourselves in case of AI-based misconduct. Our findings
have elaborated on how many AI-based misconducts are not deliberate but are ingrained in the systematic process of how AI systems
are designed. Thus, a conscious effort to ensure the inclusion and
presence of marginal communities is important as we are in the
infancy of the AI ecosystem and we emphasized it in our AI principles. AI literacy is also important among the general people as well
as policy developers who often perceive AI-based systems beyond
their capabilities (e.g., being flawless or being magical). Improving
the educational curriculum might be a good option to start with
as a previous study suggested introducing ethics study in global
CS education [103]. As the Government involvement is strong and
authoritative in South Asian countries, the AI products and corresponding data require an independent oversight body. The AI
ecosystem being in its infancy provides a great opportunity for us
to ensure we can take advantage of AI-based products in positive
ways in coming days through adequate AI ethics policy design,
implementation and deployment.
6 Conclusion
The future trajectory of AI development and its societal implications
remain uncertain, with the potential for both significant benefits
and detrimental impacts. Acknowledging the complexities of AI
adoption, this study emphasizes the necessity of context-specific AI
ethics frameworks, particularly in regions like Bangladesh, where
socio-economic, cultural, and governance-related challenges hinder the implementation of responsible AI practices. Our research
identified critical knowledge gaps, including concerns about data
protection, humanitarian issues such as wage disparities among
annotators, and a lack of public awareness. To address these challenges, we proposed an AI4Bangladesh roadmap, incorporating
stakeholder perspectives on key AI ethics principles such as fairness, explainability, and accountability, alongside region-specific
needs like independent oversight to mitigate surveillance concerns.
We propose 7 principles along with recommendations from our
stakeholders on AI related policy making in our work. These findings underscore the urgent need for targeted interventions and
policy initiatives tailored to Bangladesh’s context, while also offering a foundation for other regions with emerging AI ecosystems
or where the majority of the population lacks advanced AI literacy.
The work thus contributes to the broader discourse on inclusive
and equitable AI governance in the Global South, advancing the
discussion to bridge global principles with local concerns.

Know Your Users: Towards Explainable AI in Bangladesh
Farzana Islam
Department of Electrical and
Computer Engineering
North South University
Dhaka, Bangladesh
farzana.islam01@northsouth.edu
Tasmiah Tahsin Mayeesha
Department of Electrical and
Computer Engineering
North South University
Dhaka, Bangladesh
tasmiah.tahsin@northsouth.edu
Nova Ahmed
Department of Electrical and
Computer Engineering
North South University
Dhaka, Bangladesh
nova.ahmed@northsouth.edu
ABSTRACT
When we are talking about explainable AI and trying to come out
of the black box by going beyond algorithmic transparency, we are
being ignorant about a big user community. Although XAI research
has advanced over time, there hasn’t been much study done on the
development, evaluation, and application of explainability methodologies in the global south. In this paper, we focus on Bangladesh,
which is a part of the South, to understand the AI user community of
this region and show how the explainability needs are different for
different users and who should XAI focus on. Our work reflects on
the unique needs and constraints of the region and recommends potential directions for accessible and human-centered explainability
research. We argue that before developing technology and systems,
human requirements should be assessed and comprehended.
CCS CONCEPTS
• Human-centered computing → Human computer interaction
(HCI).
KEYWORDS
XAI for U; Explainable AI; user centric explanation; xai
ACM Reference Format:
Farzana Islam, Tasmiah Tahsin Mayeesha, and Nova Ahmed. 2024. Know
Your Users: Towards Explainable AI in Bangladesh. InCompanion of the 2024
ACM International Joint Conference on Pervasive and Ubiquitous Computing
(UbiComp Companion ’24), October 5–9, 2024, Melbourne, VIC, Australia.
ACM, New York, NY, USA, 4 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3675094.3679002
1 INTRODUCTION
In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has become the backbone of digital assistance in terms of everything and is accessible
through cell phones easily. AI is the primary force behind developing technologies like generative AI, big data, robotics, and the
Internet of Things (IoT). With open AI’s recent achievements, including GPT-4, the biggest and most sophisticated AI model for
language processing available, which has been applied to many
different tasks such as chatbots, text summarization, and language
translation, generative AI has reached a considerably higher level.

Not only that, but AI is becoming more and more commonplace and
assisting with important human decisions, including early disease
detection of deadly disease cancer and stroke [7, 8]. Therefore, AI
must be understandable to its end-users, but the machine’s inability
to explain its actions and reasoning for the decisions might limit the
acceptability of these systems. Due to these difficulties, explainable
AI (XAI) research is becoming more popular. XAI makes it possible
for human users to understand the rationale behind the output
produced by AI-driven machine learning (ML) algorithms.
Hence, the XAI system should be able to describe its capabilities
and understandings, what it has done, what it is doing right now,
and what will happen next [6]. The majority of XAI explanations
still lack usability, practical interpretability, and effectiveness for actual users [1, 19, 33, 34]. The XAI end users are those who depend on
decisions, recommendations, or actions made by an AI system [5].
Depending on the community context, there are numerous ways to
evaluate and operationalize the XAI systems. To make XAI more
explainable from a socio-technical perspective to a human-centered
perspective, much research has been conducted to understand the
user needs [ 3, 32]. Research addressing the sociotechnical challenges resulting from the usage of AI systems in the Global North
has rapidly increased in recent years [20]. However, the majority of
existing literature on XAI predominantly concentrates on research
conducted within Western geography or context [9]. Consequently,
there is a discernible scarcity of studies examining the application
of XAI in other geographical regions. Very little or no research
has been done to situate or ground explainability in the context of
the south, especially in Bangladesh. In India, studies are designed
to understand what explainability means for the underprivileged,
marginalized, and unlettered population in rural areas [28]. Urge
has also been seen in the work of Ehsan et al. [ 3] to identify the
different ‘whos’ (relevant stakeholders and end users) to understand their needs since actionable explanations can inform the
user to take better actions and help them to make the AI systems
accountable.
Making explainability meaningful and accessible for all users,
from developers to end users, in both esteemed and marginalized
communities is still a challenge. In our work, we are focusing on the
South, particularly Bangladesh. Bangladesh is the second largest
South Asian country economically. Moreover, the nation’s geographic position naturally positions it as a key component of the
US, India, Japan, and Australia’s Indo-Pacific strategy. The eighthmost populous nation in the world is Bangladesh, where 77.36
million people are using the internet and is a technology-emergent
country[12]. All things considered, AI is widely used in Bangladesh.
Some examples of this include ride-sharing, chatbots, natural language processing (NLP) for Bengali, hotel and ticket booking, and

real-time mapping. Since the country is gradually moving onto AI
era there is a great opportunity to use explainable AI to ensure
fair usage of technology. We aim to enlighten the XAI community
about the end users and their explainability needs in this region
to help the developers re-imagine the explainable methods in the
South to make user-centered explanations for AI-driven systems.
2 XAI PERSPECTIVE FROM SOUTH
XAI aims to provide explanations to the end users of AI products
who are dependent on the system’s actions, decisions, and recommendations. There are various kinds of users, from the development
phase to uses of the system [ 13]. An expert - who have enough
domain-specific knowledge; critic is someone who expresses evaluations and opinions about different kinds of creative works, including AI systems, music, film, and art or operator those who are
adept at using AI techniques to produce useful outcomes, intelligence analysts, - who have strong ability to solve problems, and
civilian society including labour unions, religious organisations,
indigenous groups, humanitarian organisations, non-governmental
organisations (NGOs) are examples of different types of users. They
also have variations according to their educational background and
profession. On the other hand, a developer who build, design, and
deploy AI systems and models or test operator who checks the
system’s functionality needs to know where there might be room
for improvement may be one of the users who requests an explanation of the system. Policymakers, whose responsibility is to further
serve the needs of a wide range of stakeholders might attempt to
gauge the system’s fairness, could be yet another user group. Each
user group might have a different demand for the explanatory style
that they find to be the most efficient to understand. The end users
(local people) might need different types of explanations according
to their needs, context, culture, education, and digital literacy level.
While the XAI community is focused on making AI systems
more explainable to end users, a parallel, underserved population
exists in the Global South. These individuals, often lacking basic
literacy, are nevertheless engaged with various AI-driven products
in their daily lives. These works so far has been centered around
global north and very little is known about how XAI techniques
have been designed, deployed, or tested with communities in the
Global South. On the other side few works that focused on XAI in
global South, most of the work was conducted in India, with less
focus on other South Asian regions, Latin America, or Africa, and
no work focused on Bangladesh. Only 3 out of 16 reviewed papers
engaged with stakeholders or end users in their work [ 4, 14, 20].
Nearly all papers in the survey used explainability methods such
as LIME or SHAP to explain how the features of the dataset contribute to the prediction by the model. LIME is a model-agnostic
method that explains complex "black-box" model predictions by
building a simple model around each prediction to identify key factors to explain individual explanations [24]. SHAP measures each
feature’s contribution to a model’s prediction using game theory
[16]. However, these methods require significant technical knowledge to understand and interpret them and might be difficult for
local users. In a research study it has been seen that AI researchers
and practitioners working on social impact problems and engaging
with users in the Global South, participants mentioned while they
knew of XAI techniques, they lacked domain expertise, faced challenges in incorporating XAI to their workflow and perceived XAI as
less useful for users with limited AI and digital literacy. The authors
encouraged more work to understand what novice AI users need
explained from AI systems to promote user agency [22]. Previous
work suggests that in the absence of an explanation provided to
the users, users often form incorrect mental models of how AI is
working under the hood, which influences their decision-making
[21].
Despite the huge number of XAI techniques, most of them are
still challenging to comprehend due to the absence of humancentered design that meets human needs [32]. With literacy, there
is another main reason for this: a lack of knowledge about AI and
technology. Local users find technical stuff complex, so they simply
like to ignore it. For this, even with technical explanations, users
must be given relevant domain knowledge (e.g., what a feature
signifies) and a broad awareness of how AI functions to attain practical understanding. Also, the "West" and "Global North" dominate
AI design, development, and research [25]. Often, limited resources
to develop region-specific AI tools make it difficult to produce their
own AI systems, and these countries greatly depend on the products
made by more technologically resourceful countries like the North.
Bangladesh is a country full of diversity and different educational
backgrounds. Instead of concentrating on how people use technologies only, XAI might consider what explainability, independence,
and sovereignty (authority) mean to people from various backgrounds in this marginalized community. The same explanation
that can satisfy a young businessperson, educator, or practitioner -a
licensed individual who is legally allowed to offer services without
being directly supervised might not be able to satisfy an older user
with the same background. In the South Asian region, it is often
found that female users are not very proficient with technology
and face barriers such as lack of access and privacy[26, 30]. For this
reason, they might need different explanations depending on the
use cases.
3 TOW ARDS EXPLAINABILITY IN
BANGLADESH
One of the biggest existing challenges with AI systems in Bangladesh
is that majority of the current systems are created with little or
no explainability, highlighting the power dynamics between system developers and underprivileged groups who are using these
systems. XAI techniques have been used in many AI-related research in Bangladesh in novel setting, such as using SHAP values
to explain breast cancer classification [ 11], flood prediction [ 17]
and student performance prediction [ 18]. Both SHAP and LIME
techniques have been used to predict solar irradiation [27] and to
model anxiety level of students in Bangladesh [10]. However, these
works are done in research setting and have not been deployed to
end users. As the following example demonstrates, end users in
many industries, including healthcare and agriculture, will profit
from the usage of explainability in AI systems.
Bangladesh’s economy mostly depends on agriculture, and there
has been a lot of advancement happening in recent times in this
sector, and now it is in the era of using digital agriculture tools. A
pilot study has been conducted on over 260 farmers from seven
891

Know Your Users: Towards Explainable AI in Bangladesh UbiComp Companion ’24, October 5–9, 2024, Melbourne, VIC, Australia
districts of Bangladesh to understand the outcomes of these farming tools introduced beforehand [31]. From the study, it has been
seen that female farmers are less likely to use these tools than men
because of low education levels. Their knowledge of the tool’s functionality was also constrained, which made them less interested
or no interest in using these tools. So there is a big question of
how can we create additional interventions that take into account
the needs of women and eventually persuade them to use these
tools. An app is in use that allows farmers to detect crop disease
with a simple picture with computer vision techniques, but there
is no explanation given to the users about the process. Some of
the farmers said, in terms of full trust, they are very curious to
learn about the processes of this magical output from the images.
Furthermore, no locals have developed these tools, and nobody is
available to respond to their inquiries. Their lack of clarity makes it
difficult to convince the farmers to use them. They might be interested in employing these tools, as they can identify the percentage
of the diagnosis that was likely caused by natural reason and the
percentage that was caused by improper management if the model
had been better created for explainability.
In a prior work, XAI was used to aid community health workers
in rural India with visual and written explanations which helped to
develop a more nuanced understanding of AI based predictions and
improved their occupational abilities. Researchers recommended
interactive visual heuristics and written explanations to promote active learning from the health workers who were the end users with
limited digital literacy to operate an AI driven child malnutrition
prediction tool [29].
Hence, we suggest that the human-centered XAI study should
start with people rather than technology as what is perceived as
reliable or useful by AI experts may differ greatly from what is
considered reliable or useful by novice end-users. Giving human
needs top priority when developing new technologies is also discussed and recommended in the work of Christine P Lee [15]. While
designing mobile financial service (MFS) applications for the lowliterate, marginalized communities in Bangladesh, authors found
that these users face unique challenges, such as not understanding the meaning of common icons and forgetting the steps while
operating specific applications. Some users derived the interpretation of icons from their cultural context, for example matching
the settings icon with a tractor wheel and the music icon with a
spoon, thus the researchers recommended the usage of culturally
relevant icons and streamlining the workflow of the applications
for the low literate user base [ 23]. For this demographic even if
we use common XAI techniques such as provision of graphs for
explainability, we need to simplify and contextualize them to obtain
user centered explanations. One way could be to design tools with
understandable language and additional features targeting users
at various literacy levels. With language for the people who have
no literacy, there could be added visuals, storytelling, voice based
features and interactive dashboards. People who are tends to learn
by observing or seeing how others are doing video demonstrations
is a way to provide locals with an adaptive and self-explanatory
explanation of the systems’ outputs and usage. We can also consider other ideas for offline setting with limited and slow internet
access in many parts of rural Bangladesh, such as sending sms for
queries on specific predictions. Using analogies such as utilizing
tangible and familiar objects or processes to explain AI concepts
may help the unlettered user demographics. Doing user research,
particularly using qualitative techniques early on (such as creating personas, task models, and stakeholder engagement), can be
another useful way to enhance acceptance. XAI researchers should
identify certain intended user groups and design XAI solutions
to fulfil their requirements. Individual users, including technical
specialists, non-experts, and AI professionals, should use the XAI
system in certain situations with specific requirements. While the
recommendations in the paper are specific to the concerns of the
users in Bangladesh, these considerations will also prove beneficial
to other South Asian nations that share comparable demographic
characteristics, as discussed in the work of Bloom DE et al. [2].
To know about the user needs specifically in this region, we
plan to conduct a mixed-method study. With an interactive strategy, we hope to identify the challenges minorities face in utilizing
explainable AI and work with them to co-design the concept of
explainability in relation to dealing with consequential AI systems.
The XAI system will be modified, and a framework will be developed based on the results of this formative research to offer the
target participants a meaningful answer. Later on, we will evaluate
the developed framework with the same participants to assess the
system’s potential.
4 CONCLUSION
With growing AI tools and decision models, proper user-centric
explanations are needed for wider acceptance and to address responsible AI practice. In this work, we contend that further work
is required to comprehend XAI system users, particularly using
improved user requirements, to increase its practical effectiveness.
While developing the systems, marginalized communities’ needs
should also be considered, and explainability should come from the
concept of one-size-fits-all.
